brief.topic: Why a Rarely Seen Item Can Carry More Weight

s01: A sample can favor some items and still estimate a total fairly.
Imagine three items with values two, four, and six. Their true total is twelve.
Choose exactly one. The first has chance one half, and the others one quarter each.
The observed value alone averages only three point five.
Instead divide the observed value by its chance of inclusion.
The possible estimates become four, sixteen, and twenty four.
Weight these by one half, one quarter, and one quarter. The average is twelve.
Each item contributes its value divided by its chance, but only when it appears.
In expectation, that chance cancels. Add across items and the true total returns. This is the Horvitz Thompson idea.
Now make the last item impossible to sample.
No finite weight can recover a value that is never observed without extra assumptions.
Known positive inclusion probabilities are essential. And unbiased means right on average, not right in every sample. Our three estimates already showed the variation.

Choose exactly one. The first has chance one half, and the others one quarter each. The observed value alone averages only three point five.

Instead divide the observed value by its chance of inclusion. The possible estimates become four, sixteen, and twenty four. Weight these by one half, one quarter, and one quarter. The average is twelve.

Each item contributes its value divided by its chance, but only when it appears. In expectation, that chance cancels. Add across items and the true total returns. This is the Horvitz Thompson idea.

Now make the last item impossible to sample. No finite weight can recover a value that is never observed without extra assumptions. Known positive inclusion probabilities are essential. And unbiased means right on average, not right in every sample. Our three estimates already showed the variation.
